source_evidence.anchor: Proposition 2.7.1, properties (a)–(d), plus the absolute-constant-factor qualification
source_evidence.observation: For a random variable X, sub-exponential tail, moment, and absolute-value MGF conditions (a)–(d) are equivalent, with their positive parameters differing by at most an absolute constant factor; in particular (a) is P{|X| ≥ t} ≤ 2 exp(−t/K₁) for all t ≥ 0, and (d) is E exp(|X|/K₄) ≤ 2.

A random variable satisfying one of Proposition 2.7.1(a)–(d) is called sub-exponential, and equation (2.21) defines ‖X‖_{ψ₁} = inf{t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) ≤ 2}. The preceding sentence instead calls this ‘the smallest K₃ in property 3.’

source_evidence.anchor: prose immediately before Lemma 2.7.6 and Lemma 2.7.6 with its proof
source_evidence.observation: The source says any sub-gaussian distribution is sub-exponential. Lemma 2.7.6 says X is sub-gaussian if and only if X² is sub-exponential and states ‖X²‖_{ψ₁} = ‖X‖_{ψ₂}²; its proof identifies ‖X‖_{ψ₂} as inf{L > 0 : E exp(X²/L²) ≤ 2}.

contract_plain_english: Example 2.7.8 says that sub-gaussian random variables, their squares (for instance g² when g ∼ N(μ, σ)), exponential distributions, and Poisson distributions are sub-exponential. [PDF p. 23, printed p. 34; anchor: Example 2.7.8 opening paragraph] It defines X ∼ Exp(λ), for λ > 0, as a non-negative random variable with P{X ≥ t} = e^(−λt) for all t ≥ 0, and then displays E X = 1/λ, Var(X) = 1/λ², and ‖X‖_{ψ₁} = C/λ, while its prose calls the relevant three quantities the mean, standard deviation, and ψ₁ norm and says they are of order 1/λ. [PDF p. 23, printed p. 34; anchor: exponential-law definition through ‘(Check this!)’] The ψ₁ gauge in the surrounding definition is inf{t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) ≤ 2}, and the square example is supported by ‖X²‖_{ψ₁} = ‖X‖_{ψ₂}². [PDF p. 22, printed p. 33; anchors: equation (2.21) and Lemma 2.7.6] The unbound C, the normal-parameter convention, the ψ₁ definition's inconsistent prose reference to K₃/property 3, and the standard-deviation-versus-variance wording are left unresolved because the cited source does not resolve them.
